_comment: Seed guides for the FinVerse RAG store (M4). Each document is indexed ONCE by the owner through the `rag` Edge Function (shared: true), which chunks the content and generates embeddings at index time — no embeddings are stored here. Content is evergreen and generic: no market prices, no return figures, no interest rates. See docs/MIGRATION.md §9 for the indexing steps.

documents.content: A Systematic Investment Plan (SIP) is a way to invest a fixed amount of money at regular intervals — usually every month — into a mutual fund. Instead of investing one large sum at once, you invest small amounts steadily over time. When markets fall, your fixed amount buys more units; when markets rise, it buys fewer. This is called rupee-cost averaging, and it removes the need to guess the right time to invest. A SIP is a habit, not a product: it works with equity funds, debt funds, and hybrid funds alike. You can usually start, pause, increase, decrease, or stop a SIP at any time, and there is no penalty for stopping. A SIP does not guarantee returns — the value of your investment still rises and falls with the market. What it guarantees is discipline: regular investing, in good months and bad, without having to decide each time.
documents.title: What is a SIP?

documents.content: An Equated Monthly Instalment (EMI) is the fixed amount you pay every month to repay a loan — a home loan, car loan, or personal loan. Each EMI has two parts: interest on the outstanding loan amount, and a part that reduces the principal you owe. Early in the loan, most of your EMI goes towards interest; towards the end, most of it goes towards the principal. This is called a reducing-balance loan: interest is charged only on what you still owe, so any extra payment you make directly reduces the principal and saves future interest. Missing an EMI usually attracts a late fee and can hurt your credit score, which affects your ability to borrow in future. Before taking a loan, check that the EMI leaves you enough room for essentials, savings, and emergencies — a loan you can barely afford becomes a burden the moment income dips.
documents.title: What is an EMI?

documents.content: The Public Provident Fund (PPF) is a government-backed long-term savings scheme. You open an account at a bank or post office and deposit money each year, up to the prevailing annual limit. The scheme runs for 15 years from the first deposit and can be extended in blocks of five years. The interest rate is set by the government and reviewed periodically, so it changes over time rather than staying fixed. PPF enjoys tax benefits under current rules: contributions qualify for deduction, the interest earned is tax-free, and the maturity amount is tax-free. Partial withdrawals are allowed only after a few years and under specific conditions, and loans can be taken against the balance in the early years. PPF suits money you will not need for a long time — it is a savings tool, not an emergency fund, because the money is locked away.
documents.title: What is PPF?

documents.content: An Equity Linked Savings Scheme (ELSS) is a mutual fund that invests mainly in equities and qualifies for tax deduction under Section 80C, up to the prevailing limit. Its lock-in period is three years — the shortest among tax-saving options — which means you cannot withdraw your money before three years from the date of each investment. Because it invests in the stock market, its returns are market-linked: they can be higher than fixed-income options in good years and negative in bad ones. There is no guaranteed return. You can invest in ELSS as a lump sum or through a monthly SIP; with a SIP, each monthly instalment has its own three-year lock-in starting from its investment date. ELSS suits investors who can leave the money untouched for at least three years and are comfortable with market ups and downs.
documents.title: What is ELSS?

documents.content: An emergency fund is money set aside for unexpected events: a job loss, a medical bill, an urgent home repair. The usual guidance is three to six months of essential expenses — rent, food, bills, transport — kept somewhere safe and easy to reach, such as a savings account. It is not an investment: the goal is not growth but availability, so it should not be in stocks or anything whose value can fall when you need it. Keep it separate from your everyday spending money so you are not tempted to dip into it. If you use it, rebuilding it becomes the priority before other goals. The size depends on your situation: a single income, irregular earnings, or dependents all argue for a larger cushion. An emergency fund turns a crisis into an inconvenience — without one, the same event often becomes debt.
documents.title: Emergency fund basics

documents.content: The FinVerse investment readiness score rates how ready you are to invest, from 0 to 100. It is computed from seven factors, each worth a fixed share of the score: emergency fund coverage (20 points), savings rate (20), debt-to-income (15), budget discipline (10), fixed-cost ratio (10), portfolio concentration (15), and volatility (10). Emergency fund coverage is full at six months of expenses saved; savings rate is full at a 20 percent average savings rate. The score bands are: 75 and above means Ready to invest, 50 to 74 means Almost ready, 30 to 49 means Build foundations first, and below 30 means Not yet — protect cash first. A factor that cannot be measured — for example debt-to-income when no debt is recorded — is shown as unmeasured and never scored as zero; the score is rescaled over the factors that could be measured. The score is a guide, not a verdict: it tells you which foundations to strengthen before putting more money into investments.
documents.title: How the FinVerse readiness score works

documents.content: An index fund simply tracks a market index, such as the NIFTY 50: it buys the same stocks in the same proportions and aims to match the index's returns. An active fund has a manager who picks stocks trying to beat the index. Index funds usually charge much lower fees, because there is no stock-picking to pay for — and fees compound over years, so a small difference in cost becomes a large difference in outcome. Active funds can beat the index in some years, but doing so consistently is hard, and past outperformance does not predict future results. Neither kind of fund guarantees returns: both rise and fall with the market. The practical question is not which is better in theory, but what you are paying for: with an index fund you pay little and accept market returns; with an active fund you pay more for the chance — not the promise — of beating the market.
documents.title: Index funds vs active funds

documents.content: Diversification means spreading your investments across different assets, sectors, and companies so that no single failure can sink your portfolio. If all your money is in one stock and that company stumbles, your whole portfolio stumbles with it; if it is spread across many stocks, one bad performer is a small dent. The same idea applies across asset types: equities, debt, and cash behave differently in different conditions, so holding a mix smooths the ride. Diversification reduces concentration risk — the risk that one bet goes wrong. It does not eliminate market risk: in a broad market fall, diversified portfolios fall too, just usually by less. And it does not guarantee a profit. A simple check is concentration: if one holding is a large share of your portfolio, you are betting heavily on it, whether you meant to or not.
documents.title: What is diversification?
